extracted.intended_audience: scientists, students of logic and scientific method, experimentalists, and philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts prescriptive principles and methodological standards for logical reasoning, induction, experiment, measurement, probability, classification, and hypothesis-use as presented in a treatise on scientific method and formal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceed from the known to the unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper course of reasoning is to proceed from the known to the unknown — from the evident to the obscure — from the material and palpable to the subtle and refined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-established, precise results (especially from physical sciences) as the practice-ground for developing methods of reasoning that can be applied to less methodical branches; avoid starting with speculation divorced from solid evidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of methods of reasoning (Scientific Method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific Method consists of general methods of inductive investigation and logical procedure which scientific men ought to be able to describe and study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit the implicit reasoning used in successful sciences; analyze the processes (deduction, induction, hypothesis, verification) rather than rely solely on ad hoc empirical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Logic as foundation for quantitative induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The more elaborate processes of quantitative induction have their necessary foundation in the simpler science of Formal Logic (including the Fundamental Laws of Thought and the Principle of Substitution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and use formal logical principles (logical alphabet, combinational logic) before or alongside quantitative methods; view combinational logic as foreshadowing complex inductive procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The all-important Principle of Substitution (objects/things that can be substituted one for another without affecting truth are treated as identical) underlies reasoning and can serve as a fundamental axiom for deduction and mathematical inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use substitution as a core rule in logical manipulations and derivations; be aware of philosophical issues (definition vs axiom) but treat substitution as operationally central to inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is inverse deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no distinct method of induction contrasted with deduction; induction is simply an inverse employment of deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach inductive problems as inverse problems of deductive systems; apply rules of deduction 'in reverse' and justify inductive steps via inverse-method analyses rather than treating induction as purely empirical aggregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of hypotheses as essential to inductive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical anticipation of nature is an essential part of inductive inquiry; the Newtonian method combines deductive hypotheses with elaborate experimental verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form representative hypotheses to guide experiments and predictions; do not expect raw data alone to yield laws without imaginative hypothesis formation followed by rigorous testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of probability as essential part of logical method
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of probability enables estimation and calculation of 'quantities of knowledge' and is essential to logical method; the inverse method of probabilities is conceived as the true principle of inductive procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify the logical value of inductive results using probability theory and the inverse (Bayesian-like) approach; accept that inductive conclusions are probabilistic, not certain.

rubrics_metrics.name: No inductive conclusions exceed probability
rubrics_metrics.description: No inductive conclusions are more than probable; the logical value of every inductive result must be determined (consciously or unconsciously) according to principles of the inverse method of probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express certainty levels numerically where possible; avoid categorical claims of certainty for inductive inferences and report probable errors or confidence measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact measurement, error elimination, and probable error
rubrics_metrics.description: Exact measurement requires devices and systematic procedures by which errors are eliminated, a probable mean result attained, and the probable error of that mean ascertained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ measurement devices and protocols that reduce systematic error; compute means and probable errors; document measurement methods and error-analysis steps explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions and precautions for accurate observation and experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful experiment and accurate observation demand particular conditions and precautions (taught in a dedicated chapter) to ensure detection of quantitative laws of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with attention to controls, minimization of bias and confounders, isolation of variables, repeatability, and clear reporting of conditions; perform test experiments and controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of Approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative laws must be understood in light of the degree of quantitative approximation to truth probably attained; a theory of approximation is essential to scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always assess how close experimental/theoretical results are to true values; include approximation bounds and discuss limitations of measurements and models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by distinct methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Successive verification of an hypothesis by distinct methods of experiment yields conclusions approximating to, but never attaining, certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek independent, varied lines of evidence to corroborate hypotheses; use converging methods to increase confidence while acknowledging residual uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of the experimentalist
rubrics_metrics.description: There are characteristic intellectual and methodological qualities of the successful experimentalist (discussed in a chapter), illustrating inverse deduction as their logical method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate traits such as careful observation, imagination in hypothesis formation, attention to systematic error-reduction, and rigorous testing; training should emphasise these character traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precautions in generalisation and analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: When inferring from one case to another or from one part of the universe to another, special precautions are required; the validity of such inferences rests on the inverse method of probabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate similarity, consider alternative explanations, quantify how representative a sample/case is, and apply probability-based assessments before generalising; avoid rash extrapolation from limited cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and explanation of exceptional phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Outstanding or exceptional facts must be carefully examined and explained by considering various modes of explanation rather than being dismissed or immediately incorporated into general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate anomalies rigorously (measurement error, overlooked variables, novel phenomena); use anomalies to refine, reject, or extend hypotheses rather than as mere outliers to be ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification grounded in Formal Logic
rubrics_metrics.description: All classification is fundamentally carried out upon the principles of Formal Logic and the Logical Alphabet; classification principles should be made explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base taxonomies and classificatory schemes on clear logical criteria and definitions; make predicates, categories, and criteria explicit, and consider natural vs artificial classification distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical Alphabet and combinational logic as tools
rubrics_metrics.description: The Logical Alphabet and the combinational view of Logic provide a framework that foreshadows complex inductive procedures and can be made evident by mechanical/visual devices (logical machines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symbolic/combinational methods (and pedagogical devices) to train reasoning; employ schematic/combinatorial techniques to explore logical combinations and to test students' skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of graduated problems for logical training
rubrics_metrics.description: To test logical skill, give a series of problems graduated in difficulty so students can practise and evaluate inductive logical problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include exercises of increasing complexity in curricula; use them to assess competence in formal and inductive reasoning, including inverse-problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and units of measurement; theory of dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Units and standards of measurement must be defined; include a theory of dimensions and consider natural systems of standards (e.g., based on length/rapidity of light waves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and document consistent measurement standards; consider provisional and natural units where appropriate; discuss dimensional analysis and standards' practical implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve judgment and acknowledge limits of scientific inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific inferences have limited logical value; claims such as the 'Reign of Law' or absolute 'Uniformity of Nature' may be unverified hypotheses; interpret scientific results affirmatively but with awareness of limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreaching metaphysical conclusions from scientific results; explicitly state the domain and limitations of inferences and be cautious about extrapolating beyond data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imagination and representative hypotheses responsibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination and representative hypotheses are valuable in discovery and prediction but must be subjected to rigorous verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage creative hypothesis generation while ensuring subsequent strict experimental testing; document the origin and rationale for representative hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply rules for calculation of combinations, probabilities, inverse method, and elimination of error
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist formal rules for calculation of combinations, probabilities, execution of the inverse method, and procedures for elimination of observational error which underpin methodological practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach and use explicit computational rules (combinatorics, probability formulas, inverse inference calculations) and systematic rules for rejecting or correcting faulty observations; record procedures and justification for data elimination.
